title: Question 6
stem: Nuclei of an isotope of samarium (Sm) each contain 62 protons and 85 neutrons.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the nuclide notation in the form $^{A}_{Z}X$ for this isotope of samarium.

markscheme_points.text: resistance has decreased (and e.m.f. is unchanged)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the top number $A$ and bottom number $Z$ mean in $^{A}_{Z}X$ and how they relate to the counts of protons and neutrons given.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Build the nucleon number**
You have 62 protons and 85 neutrons sitting together in the nucleus. The top number $A$ counts all nucleons, so $$A = 62 + 85 = 147$$

Step 2: **Write the full symbol**
The bottom number $Z$ is the proton number, so $Z = 62$. Putting it together with the chemical symbol Sm gives $$^{147}_{62}\text{Sm}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain how Fig. 6.1 shows that this isotope of samarium emits $\alpha$-particles and does **not** emit $\beta$-particles.
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the shape in Fig. 6.1 - all the particles are counted at one single value of kinetic energy. What does that tell you about whether the energy is discrete or spread out?
Hint 2: Recall how alpha decay and beta decay differ: one gives every particle the same energy, the other shares energy with an antineutrino so gives a spread of energies.
parts.proper_answer: Fig. 6.1 shows a single discrete energy, characteristic of alpha-particles. Beta-particles would show a continuous range of energies, which is not seen, so no beta emission.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read what the graph is telling you**
The vertical line means a large number of particles all have exactly the same kinetic energy. There is no spread. That is a discrete, line spectrum.

Step 2: **Link to alpha and beta**
Alpha-particles are emitted with discrete energies because the decay is a two-body break-up with fixed energy sharing. So this single peak fits alpha emission: $$\text{all } \alpha \text{ have one } E_k$$ Beta decay is three-body, energy is shared randomly between the beta-particle and an antineutrino, so beta-particles show a continuous range of kinetic energies from zero up to a maximum. That continuous spread is absent here, so beta-particles are not emitted.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
This isotope of samarium decays to an isotope of neodymium (Nd).

Give the radioactive decay equation for this decay. Include the nucleon and proton numbers of **all** the particles involved.

markscheme_points.text: current means a bigger drop in p.d. across the internal resistance

hints: Hint 1: Start from your $^{147}_{62}\text{Sm}$ nucleus and remember what an alpha-particle carries away in terms of mass and charge.
Hint 2: Use conservation to find what must be left behind: subtract the alpha nucleons and protons from the parent to get the daughter Nd numbers.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Know the alpha-particle**
An alpha-particle is a helium nucleus: $$^{4}_{2}\text{He} \text{ or } ^{4}_{2}\alpha$$ It removes 4 nucleons and 2 protons from the parent.

Step 2: **Balance the decay**
Nucleon number must balance: $147 = A_{Nd} + 4$, so $A_{Nd} = 143$. Proton number (charge) must balance: $62 = Z_{Nd} + 2$, so $Z_{Nd} = 60$. The full balanced equation is: $$^{147}_{62}\text{Sm} \rightarrow ^{143}_{60}\text{Nd} + ^{4}_{2}\alpha$$

key_concepts: conservation of nucleon number and charge

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A baryon is composed of three quarks which all have different flavours. The baryon has a charge of 0.

Two of the quarks in the baryon are an up quark and a bottom quark.
parts.text: Determine, in terms of the elementary charge $e$, the charge on the third quark in the baryon.

markscheme_points.text: energy of the particles is discrete / has only one value (so must be alpha)
betas have a (continuous) range of (kinetic) energies (so can be beta)

hints: Hint 1: Write down the charges you know for the two given quarks, up and bottom, in units of $e$.
Hint 2: The three quark charges must add to the total baryon charge of zero, so work out what third value cancels the sum of the first two.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Add the known quark charges**
Recall: $$q_{up} = +\frac{2}{3}e$$ $$q_{bottom} = -\frac{1}{3}e$$ Sum so far: $$+\frac{2}{3}e - \frac{1}{3}e = +\frac{1}{3}e$$

Step 2: **Require zero total charge**
Let the third quark have charge $q$. For the baryon: $$+\frac{1}{3}e + q = 0$$ So $$q = -\frac{1}{3}e$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: State a possible flavour for the third quark in the baryon.

markscheme_points.text: $^{4}_{2}\alpha$ and Nd correct with no other extra particles on either side of equation

hints: Hint 1: The third quark must have charge $-1/3e$ and must be a different flavour from both up and bottom - which flavours carry $-1/3e$?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick a matching flavour**
Quarks with charge $-1/3e$ are down, strange and bottom. Bottom is already used and all three flavours must be different, so the third quark can be strange (down is also allowed as a different flavour from up and bottom). A common answer is the strange quark.
